sections.text: A struct groups related values under one name. Each value is a field with its own name and type.
Read a field with a dot: p.name. To change fields, the whole variable must be mut:
Add #[derive(Debug)] above a struct to print it with {:?}, or {:#?} for a tidy multi-line view:
A struct is like a form with labelled boxes: every Player has a name box, a level box and an online box.

Rust has no classes or inheritance. Data lives in structs and enums, behaviour goes in impl blocks (next lesson), and shared behaviour comes from traits. Tuple structs like struct Meters(f64); give a plain value its own type.

exercise.prompt: Create a Book with title "Dune" and pages 412, then print it as shown. It should print: Dune has 412 pages
hints: Look at how the struct is defined, then create a value with a field for each piece of data. Do that before the println!.
Create it like this: let book = Book { title: ..., pages: ... }. A String needs String::from("..."). Read fields with book.title.
Write let book = Book { title: String::from("Dune"), pages: 412 }; Then print with println!("{} has {} pages", book.title, book.pages);

quiz.question: How do you read the level field of a struct value p?
What do you need to change a field?
options: The variable must be declared mut
